diagnosis: When the seller states the farm cost, the model mostly ignores it. Its offers settle near the middle or upper part of the market's usual price range and seem anchored on that range, not on the cost or the resale value. As a result it often bids well above a low stated cost and gives away profit. For example, with a stated cost of three, a resale value of nine and prices from two to six, it offers five almost every time when three is best. Sometimes it offers at or above the resale value even though a cheaper price would be accepted, so it takes a sure loss or zero. This happens because it never compares its offer with the resale value. It does well only when the stated cost is above every profitable price, so any low offer is refused and costs nothing, or when no cost is stated and a middle price happens to be best.
method: How to choose the offer: ignore the market's usual price range and any wish to look tough; only the farm cost and the resale value matter. If the seller states the farm cost, believe it and find the cheapest listed price at or above that cost. If that price is below the resale value, offer exactly it: anything lower is refused and anything higher gives away profit. Otherwise offer the lowest listed price, which is refused or loses least. If no cost is stated, for each listed price below the resale value, take its chance of acceptance, the share of possible farm costs between the stated limits that are at or below it, times its profit, resale value minus price, and offer the price with the largest result. If no listed price is below the resale value, offer the lowest one.
